events.event_label: dsRNA affects mortality and hsp70 under semi-field conditions
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p002.s006: However, ChiLCV copies significantly increased in fas2 dsRNA-fed B. tabaci. PMC8909865.p002.s007: Transmission of ChiLCV by B. tabaci was completely inhibited post-24 h feeding on hsp70 dsRNA at 3 μg/mL. Naked hsp70 dsRNA was topically sprayed on ChiLCV-infected chilli plants like an insecticide. PMC8909865.p002.s008: 67.77% mortality of B. tabaci, 4.6-fold downregulation of hsp70 mRNA, and 1.34 × 1015-fold decreased ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci were recorded when adults were exposed to the dsRNA-treated plants under semi-field conditions. events.event_label: dsRNA and untreated control affects virus copy number
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p042.s006: When B. tabaci was fed with sterile distilled water instead of hsp70 dsRNA, the mean ChiLCV copy number was 2.22 × 1015, whereas it decreased by 35.18-fold (6.31 × 1013 copies) post-exposure to hsp70 dsRNA at 1.0 μg/mL (Figure 3c). PMC8909865.p042.s007: The virus copy number in treated B. tabaci further decreased with a gradual increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration. PMC8909865.p042.s008: At 2.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA, ChiLCV copy numbers were 6.14 × 1010 in B. tabaci i.e., 3.62 × 104-fold lower than the untreated control. PMC8909865.p042.s009: The virus copies were undetectable in B. tabaci with a further increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration to 3.0 μg/mL. The retention of ChiLCV might be completely ceased at a higher concentration of hsp70 dsRNA or beyond the detection limit using qPCR. PMC8909865.p042.s010: In contrast, the ChiLCV copy number acquired by fas2 dsRNA-treated B. tabaci was significantly higher than the untreated control (Figure 3d).

events.event_label: virus titer and transmission of ChiLCV affects leaf curl symptoms
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p046.s003: The melt curve of ChiLCV amplicon in qPCR produced specific peaks without any secondary peaks that confirmed the specificity of the reactions (Figure 4e). PMC8909865.p046.s004: When a portion of the same B. tabaci population was used for inoculation of ChiLCV in healthy chilli plants, a 75% decrease in transmission efficiency was confirmed in PCR test (Figure 4f) with no visible symptoms in the inoculated plants up to 50 days post-inoculation (Figure 4g). PMC8909865.p046.s005: Probably, the virus titer was too low in inoculated plants to produce strong visible symptoms, whereas 100% transmission and severe leaf curl symptoms were noted in plants inoculated by unexposed B. tabaci. PMC8909865.p046.s006: No transmission of ChiLCV was recorded in the plants mock-inoculated with untreated virus-free B. tabaci.

events.event_label: dsRNA affects transmission of ChiLCV and mortality under ChiLCV infection
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p051.s009: RNAi using dsRNA constructs is not suitable for field conditions due to rapid degradation and a lack of reliable delivery agents. PMC8909865.p051.s010: In the present study, for the first time, we demonstrated the efficacy of a naked dsRNA against an insect pest by spray-on application under semi-field conditions. PMC8909865.p051.s011: The dsRNA construct targeting the hsp70 gene of B. tabaci not only induced mortality in B. tabaci but also inhibited the transmission of ChiLCV from infected to healthy chilli plants by B. tabaci.

events.event_label: hsp70 and Fas2 confers tolerance to ChiLCV infection
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p052.s006: The fas2 mRNA expression level was upregulated in viruliferous B. tabaci by 2.6 and 4.518-fold in the RNA-Seq and RT-qPCR assay, respectively. PMC8909865.p052.s007: The Fas2 orthologue in mammals (NCAM) is known to serve as a receptor for the rabies virus. PMC8909865.p052.s008: Hence, we targeted to knock down these two genes, hsp70 and fas2, to induce immunity to ChiLCV infection in B. tabaci. PMC8909865.p052.s009: Conserved 128 and 150 nt stretches in the hsp70 and fas2 genes, respectively, were found to be specific to B. tabaci without any cross-reactivity to humans, mice, birds, butterflies, bees, ants, and plants. PMC8909865.p052.s010: Each produced a putative siRNA of 21 nt.

events.event_label: dsRNA exposure decreases expression of hsp70 and fas2
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p052.s018: Similarly, fas2 dsRNA at 3.0 μg/mL caused 72% mortality of B. tabaci 24 h post-feeding. PMC8909865.p052.s019: The dsRNA exposure downregulated the hsp70 and fas2 mRNA expressions by 12.85- and 8.53-fold, respectively. PMC8909865.p052.s020: The expression of an endogenous control gene was unregulated post-dsRNA exposure. PMC8909865.p052.s021: This indicated the specificity of the dsRNA constructs to target genes. events.event_label: Bta03000 and Bta02903 affects hsp70
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p053.s015: Significantly increased transmission efficiency of CLCuV was noted in B. tabaci Asia II 1 when hsp70 was silenced. PMC8909865.p053.s016: The difference may be due to the variation in virus species and B. tabaci cryptic species. PMC8909865.p053.s017: The interactions of B. tabaci with begomoviruses are not conserved and alter with cryptic species of B. tabaci and begomovirus species. PMC8909865.p053.s018: B. tabaci MEAM1 has two genes (Bta03000 and Bta02903) annotated as hsp70, and their amino acid sequences differ by 97.55%. PMC8909865.p053.s019: They might also exhibit differential responses to begomovirus infection.

events.event_label: dsRNA affects mortality and hsp70
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p054.s009: Hence, naked hsp70 dsRNA without any delivery agent was topically sprayed onto the foliage of the ChiLCV-infected chilli plant under contained semi-field conditions. PMC8909865.p054.s010: B. tabaci adults were released on the dsRNA-sprayed plants to evaluate the dsRNA’s efficacy in eradicating B. tabaci and inhibiting the transmission of ChiLCV. PMC8909865.p054.s011: Considering the extracellular degradation of dsRNA and delivery through the host plant, a 10-fold higher dose than the controlled assay was used for topical application. PMC8909865.p054.s012: A 67.77% mortality with a 4.6-fold decrease in hsp70 mRNA levels in B. tabaci exposed to the dsRNA-sprayed plants was noted after 24 h of release. PMC8909865.p054.s013: Further, 1.84 × 108-fold decreased ChiLCV copies and 75% reduced transmission of ChiLCV indicated the efficiency of topically sprayed hsp70 dsRNA in managing both the virus and its vector.

events.event_label: dsRNA affects ChiLCV and transmission of ChiLCV
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p054.s012: A 67.77% mortality with a 4.6-fold decrease in hsp70 mRNA levels in B. tabaci exposed to the dsRNA-sprayed plants was noted after 24 h of release. PMC8909865.p054.s013: Further, 1.84 × 108-fold decreased ChiLCV copies and 75% reduced transmission of ChiLCV indicated the efficiency of topically sprayed hsp70 dsRNA in managing both the virus and its vector. PMC8909865.p054.s014: Although the efficacy of topically applied naked dsRNA against plant viruses is known, this is the first evidence of its efficacy against a hemipteran insect like B. tabaci.

events.event_label: dsRNA affects ChiLCV and B. tabaci under real-field conditions
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p057.s001: In conclusion, the spray-on application of naked dsRNA targeting hsp70 of B. tabaci provides resistance to both ChiLCV and its vector, B. tabaci. PMC8909865.p057.s002: This is a novel alternative to hazardous insecticides and may be further assessed on a large scale for its efficacy under real-field conditions.

events.event_label: DNA-A component affects chilli plants and ChiLCV
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p035.s001: The identity of the virus was confirmed by sequencing the DNA-A component from infected chilli plants. PMC8909865.p035.s002: PCR amplification of the DNA-A using Begomo F and Begomo R primer produced a 2.7 kb product visualized on 1% agarose gel. PMC8909865.p035.s003: Bidirectional sequencing of the cloned products produced a 2763 nt sequence comprising complete DNA-A that showed 100% nucleotide identity to ChiLCV isolates upon BLASTn analysis. PMC8909865.p035.s004: The sequence can be retrieved by GenBank Accession No. OM513903.

events.event_label: hsp70 gene and fas2 gene is involved with siRNA
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p037.s001: A conserved 128 nt-long (2416 to 2543 nt) fragment of the hsp70 gene (~2.5 kb) and a 150 nt-long (1085 to 1234 nt) fragment of the fas2 gene (~1.4 kb) of B. tabaci were selected for dsRNA designing (Figure 1a,b). PMC8909865.p037.s002: In siRNA Wizard 3.1, the 128 nt-long B. tabaci hsp70 fragment produced a putative siRNA of 21 nt (5’-GAUCCAUCCAUGCCGUUAAUC-3’). PMC8909865.p037.s003: The 150 nt-long fas2 fragment also yielded one putative siRNA of 21 nt (5’-GGACGGAAGAAGGCAUAAUCA-3’). PMC8909865.p037.s004: The dsRNA sequence was specific to B. tabaci, and no cross-reactivity was recorded with other organisms such as Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, Aves (taxid:8782), Lepidoptera (taxid:7088), Hymenoptera (taxid:7399), Formicidae (taxid:36668), and plants (taxid:3193) in BLAST analysis.

events.event_label: dsRNA affects mRNA expression under Controlled Conditions
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p040.s003: The mRNA expression levels were significantly reduced with an increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration. PMC8909865.p040.s004: An exposure to hsp70 dsRNA at 2.0 μg/mL for 24 h significantly reduced the hsp70 mRNA expression by 11.32-fold and up to 12.85-fold when fed with 3.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA. PMC8909865.p040.s005: The fas2 mRNA expression levels were declined by 5.48-fold post-24 h feeding on fas2 dsRNA at 1.0 μg/mL. The mRNA expression levels post-hsp70 and -fas2 dsRNA feeding were almost similar at 1.0 μg/mL. The mRNA expression levels were significantly reduced up to 8.53-fold with an increase in fas2 dsRNA concentration. PMC8909865.p040.s006: The reduction in mRNA expression level was significantly higher post-hsp70 dsRNA feeding compared to fas2 dsRNA at 2.0 and 3.0 μg/mL. The primer pairs for hsp70, fas2, and β-actin did not produce any secondary peaks in the RT-qPCR melting curve analysis that indicated the specificity of the reactions (Figure 2d,e).

events.event_label: Hsp70 affects TYLCV CP and midgut epithelial cells
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p053.s003: Hsp70, along with other molecular chaperones, plays an important role in the translocation of viral proteins besides its function in viral replication, assembly, and disassembly of the viral proteins inside the hosts. PMC8909865.p053.s004: Hsp70 has been found to interact with TYLCV CP in vitro and co-localize within midgut epithelial cells. PMC8909865.p053.s005: In the present study, oral delivery of hsp70 dsRNA significantly reduced ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci Asia II 1 and its transmission to healthy chilli plants as well. PMC8909865.p053.s006: The resistance to ChiLCV in B. tabaci was enhanced at higher concentrations of hsp70 dsRNA. PMC8909865.p053.s007: ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci were imperceptible when B. tabaci fed on 3 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA for 24 h. The transmission of ChiLCV from infected to healthy plants by B. tabaci Asia II 1 was completely inhibited at 3 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA treatment under controlled conditions.

events.event_label: hsp70 affects Transmission
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p053.s009: The TYLCV titer decreased in B. tabaci Middle East Asia Minor 1 (MEAM 1) after feeding on hsp70 dsRNA-expressing tomato plants. PMC8909865.p053.s010: Transmission of TYLCV also dropped by 12% post-silencing of hsp70. PMC8909865.p053.s011: In the present study, the inability of B. tabaci Asia II 1 to retain and transmit ChiLCV post-silencing of hsp70 indicates that it might also play an important function in ChiLCV infection. PMC8909865.p053.s012: However, Gotz et al. reported an increase in TYLCV transmission upon blocking Hsp70 by anti-Hsp70 antibody in B. tabaci MEAM1. PMC8909865.p053.s013: It was hypothesized that the Hsp70-TYLCV interaction mediates the degradation of virions.

events.event_label: ChiLCV infection and fas2 affects fas2 and ChiLCV infection
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p053.s021: The Fas2 orthologue in mammals (NCAM) is known to serve as a receptor for the rabies virus. PMC8909865.p053.s022: Although NCAM promotes the penetration of the virus in cells, it suppresses virus replication via induction of Interferon-ß, which is mainly involved in innate immunity against viral infection. PMC8909865.p053.s023: Upregulation of fas2 transcripts in B. tabaci post-ChiLCV infection might be due to the innate immune response against the virus infection. PMC8909865.p053.s024: We hypothesized that fas2 has a negative regulatory role in ChiLCV infection, and thus, knocking down fas2 increased the virus titer in B. tabaci. PMC8909865.p053.s025: Hence, silencing fas2 was not considered to induce resistance to ChiLCV despite its efficacy in eradicating B. tabaci.

events.event_label: dsRNA affects transmission and leaf curl symptoms
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p159.s015: All the plants inoculated by B. tabaci fed with 1.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA were ChiLCV-positive in PCR but produced less severe symptoms of leaf curl than control. PMC8909865.p159.s016: The transmission efficiency of B. tabaci fed with 2.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA was 40%; inoculated plants produced mild leaf curl symptoms. PMC8909865.p159.s017: All the plants inoculated by B. tabaci fed with 3.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA did not produce any symptoms and were ChiLCV-negative in PCR. PMC8909865.p159.s018: For each treatment, three biological replicates were used and each replicate contained five plants.

events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p005.s015: Interrupting the interrelationship between B. tabaci and begomovirus using RNAi is a promising approach.. For successful persistent-circulative transmission, the begomovirus particles need to cross the midgut barrier of B. tabaci to circulate in hemolymph and reach the primary salivary glands. PMC8909865.p005.s016: Several proteins at the midguts of B. tabaci, such as heat shock proteins (Hsp), cyclophilins, peptidoglycan recognition protein, and a midgut protein, are known to interact with begomovirus coat protein (CP) for successful internalization. PMC8909865.p005.s017: RNA-Seq of B. tabaci in response to begomoviruses revealed significant upregulations of hsp70, fasciclin 2 (fas2), and several other transcripts. PMC8909865.p005.s018: In gene regulatory network analyses, these genes were enriched with higher degrees of interactions. PMC8909865.p005.s019: The same trend was recorded in the mRNA expression in reverse transcriptase quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) post-exposure to ChiLCV.

events.event_label: topical spray affects mortality
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p049.s001: To check the persistency in eradicating B. tabaci population by the topical spray of hsp70 dsRNA under contained semi-field conditions, fresh B. tabaci adults were released on the dsRNA-treated chilli plants at 24 h intervals. PMC8909865.p049.s002: After the first topical spray, mortality of 58.89% was recorded at 2 days. PMC8909865.p049.s003: Significant mortality (56.67%) persisted up to 8 days after the first spray (Figure 5b). PMC8909865.p049.s004: The mortality decreased to 13.33% at 10 days after the first spray. PMC8909865.p049.s006: After the second topical spray of dsRNA, the mortality percentage again rose to 75% at two days. PMC8909865.p049.s007: The highest mortality (86.67%) of B. tabaci was recorded 4 days after the second spray. PMC8909865.p049.s008: Significantly higher mortality was sustained up to 8 days after the second application and thereafter started decreasing. events.event_label: dsRNA affects mortality, Transmission of ChiLCV, hsp70, ChiLCV, and B. tabaci
events.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p002.s001: Chilli leaf curl virus (ChiLCV; genus: Begomovirus), transmitted by Bemisia tabaci (Gennadius) (Hemiptera: Aleyrodidae) in a persistent-circulative manner, is a major constraint in chilli production. PMC8909865.p002.s002: The present study demonstrates for the first time that a topical spray of naked double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) on chilli plants causes mortality and inability to acquire and transmit ChiLCV in B. tabaci. PMC8909865.p002.s003: dsRNA targeting heat shock protein 70 (hsp70) and fasciclin 2 (fas2) of B. tabaci Asia II 1 was first assessed under controlled conditions through oral delivery. PMC8909865.p002.s004: Hsp70 and fas2 dsRNA resulted in up to 82.22% and 72% mortality of B. tabaci and around 12.4- and 8.5-fold decreases in mRNA levels, respectively, 24 h post-ingestion. PMC8909865.p002.s006: However, ChiLCV copies significantly increased in fas2 dsRNA-fed B. tabaci. PMC8909865.p002.s007: Transmission of ChiLCV by B. tabaci was completely inhibited post-24 h feeding on hsp70 dsRNA at 3 μg/mL. Naked hsp70 dsRNA was topically sprayed on ChiLCV-infected chilli plants like an insecticide. PMC8909865.p002.s008: 67.77% mortality of B. tabaci, 4.6-fold downregulation of hsp70 mRNA, and 1.34 × 1015-fold decreased ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci were recorded when adults were exposed to the dsRNA-treated plants under semi-field conditions. PMC8909865.p002.s009: Foliar application of naked dsRNA reduced the ChiLCV transmission by 75% without any visible symptoms in the inoculated plants. PMC8909865.p002.s010: A total of 2 consecutive sprays of dsRNA provided significant protection to B. tabaci for up to 20 days under semi-field conditions.

For successful persistent-circulative transmission, the begomovirus particles need to cross the midgut barrier of B. tabaci to circulate in hemolymph and reach the primary salivary glands. PMC8909865.p005.s016: Several proteins at the midguts of B. tabaci, such as heat shock proteins (Hsp), cyclophilins, peptidoglycan recognition protein, and a midgut protein, are known to interact with begomovirus coat protein (CP) for successful internalization. PMC8909865.p005.s017: RNA-Seq of B. tabaci in response to begomoviruses revealed significant upregulations of hsp70, fasciclin 2 (fas2), and several other transcripts. PMC8909865.p005.s018: In gene regulatory network analyses, these genes were enriched with higher degrees of interactions. PMC8909865.p005.s019: The same trend was recorded in the mRNA expression in reverse transcriptase quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) post-exposure to ChiLCV.

evidence_context_sentences.text: Chilli leaf curl virus (ChiLCV; genus: Begomovirus), transmitted by Bemisia tabaci (Gennadius) (Hemiptera: Aleyrodidae) in a persistent-circulative manner, is a major constraint in chilli production.

The present study demonstrates for the first time that a topical spray of naked double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) on chilli plants causes mortality and inability to acquire and transmit ChiLCV in B. tabaci.
dsRNA targeting heat shock protein 70 (hsp70) and fasciclin 2 (fas2) of B. tabaci Asia II 1 was first assessed under controlled conditions through oral delivery.
Hsp70 and fas2 dsRNA resulted in up to 82.22% and 72% mortality of B. tabaci and around 12.4- and 8.5-fold decreases in mRNA levels, respectively, 24 h post-ingestion.

evidence_context_sentences.text: Interrupting the interrelationship between B. tabaci and begomovirus using RNAi is a promising approach.. For successful persistent-circulative transmission, the begomovirus particles need to cross the midgut barrier of B. tabaci to circulate in hemolymph and reach the primary salivary glands.

Several proteins at the midguts of B. tabaci, such as heat shock proteins (Hsp), cyclophilins, peptidoglycan recognition protein, and a midgut protein, are known to interact with begomovirus coat protein (CP) for successful internalization.
RNA-Seq of B. tabaci in response to begomoviruses revealed significant upregulations of hsp70, fasciclin 2 (fas2), and several other transcripts.
In gene regulatory network analyses, these genes were enriched with higher degrees of interactions.

evidence_context_sentences.text: A conserved 128 nt-long (2416 to 2543 nt) fragment of the hsp70 gene (~2.5 kb) and a 150 nt-long (1085 to 1234 nt) fragment of the fas2 gene (~1.4 kb) of B. tabaci were selected for dsRNA designing (Figure 1a,b).
In siRNA Wizard 3.1, the 128 nt-long B. tabaci hsp70 fragment produced a putative siRNA of 21 nt (5’-GAUCCAUCCAUGCCGUUAAUC-3’).
The 150 nt-long fas2 fragment also yielded one putative siRNA of 21 nt (5’-GGACGGAAGAAGGCAUAAUCA-3’).

The dsRNA sequence was specific to B. tabaci, and no cross-reactivity was recorded with other organisms such as Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, Aves (taxid:8782), Lepidoptera (taxid:7088), Hymenoptera (taxid:7399), Formicidae (taxid:36668), and plants (taxid:3193) in BLAST analysis.

evidence.text: Significantly higher mortality (62 and 72%) of B. tabaci adults was recorded when 2.0 and 3.0 μg/mL fas2 dsRNA was orally delivered to B. tabaci under controlled laboratory conditions.

relations.evidence_context_text: PMC8909865.p039.s006: Oral delivery of fas2 dsRNA at 1.0 μg/mL exhibited 39.33% mean mortality after 24 h (Figure 2b). evidence_context_sentences.text: Oral delivery of fas2 dsRNA at 1.0 μg/mL exhibited 39.33% mean mortality after 24 h (Figure 2b).
Significantly higher mortality (62 and 72%) of B. tabaci adults was recorded when 2.0 and 3.0 μg/mL fas2 dsRNA was orally delivered to B. tabaci under controlled laboratory conditions.
At all doses, the mortality of B. tabaci post-fas2 dsRNA exposure was significantly lower than the hsp70 dsRNA at p  <  0.05.
However, no morpho-deformities were observed in killed B. tabaci adults either with hsp70 or fas2 dsRNA.

evidence_context_sentences.text: The mRNA expression levels were significantly reduced with an increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration.

evidence.text: The virus copy number in treated B. tabaci further decreased with a gradual increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration.
At 2.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA, ChiLCV copy numbers were 6.14 × 1010 in B. tabaci i.e., 3.62 × 104-fold lower than the untreated control.

evidence_context_sentences.text: The surviving B. tabaci adults post-exposure to dsRNA-treated plants were further assessed for ChiLCV acquisition and transmission efficiency.

When a portion of the same B. tabaci population was used for inoculation of ChiLCV in healthy chilli plants, a 75% decrease in transmission efficiency was confirmed in PCR test (Figure 4f) with no visible symptoms in the inoculated plants up to 50 days post-inoculation (Figure 4g).

67.77% mortality of B. tabaci, 4.6-fold downregulation of hsp70 mRNA, and 1.34 × 1015-fold decreased ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci were recorded when adults were exposed to the dsRNA-treated plants under semi-field conditions.
In contrast, the ChiLCV copy number acquired by fas2 dsRNA-treated B. tabaci was significantly higher than the untreated control (Figure 3d).
The dsRNA construct targeting the hsp70 gene of B. tabaci not only induced mortality in B. tabaci but also inhibited the transmission of ChiLCV from infected to healthy chilli plants by B. tabaci.
A 67.77% mortality of adult B. tabaci was recorded post-24 h exposure to dsRNA-treated plants (Figure 4a).

The present study demonstrates for the first time that a topical spray of naked double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) on chilli plants causes mortality and inability to acquire and transmit ChiLCV in B. tabaci.

entities.selected_description: Any biological process that results in permanent cessation of all vital functions of a cell. A cell should be considered dead when any one of the following molecular or morphological criteria is met: (1) the cell has lost the integrity of its plasma membrane; (2) the cell, including its nucleus, has undergone complete fragmentation into discrete bodies (frequently referred to as apoptotic bodies). The cell corpse (or its fragments) may be engulfed by an adjacent cell in vivo, but engulfment of whole cells should not be considered a strict criteria to define cell death as, under some circumstances, live engulfed cells can be released from phagosomes (see PMID:18045538).

3.5. Effect of Topical Spray of hsp70 dsRNA on Mortality and Virus Transmission by B. tabaci under Semi-Field Conditions

sentences.text: Topical Spray of dsRNA Induces Mortality and Inhibits Chilli Leaf Curl Virus Transmission by Bemisia tabaci Asia II 1
Chilli leaf curl virus (ChiLCV; genus: Begomovirus), transmitted by Bemisia tabaci (Gennadius) (Hemiptera: Aleyrodidae) in a persistent-circulative manner, is a major constraint in chilli production.

The present study demonstrates for the first time that a topical spray of naked double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) on chilli plants causes mortality and inability to acquire and transmit ChiLCV in B. tabaci.
dsRNA targeting heat shock protein 70 (hsp70) and fasciclin 2 (fas2) of B. tabaci Asia II 1 was first assessed under controlled conditions through oral delivery.
Hsp70 and fas2 dsRNA resulted in up to 82.22% and 72% mortality of B. tabaci and around 12.4- and 8.5-fold decreases in mRNA levels, respectively, 24 h post-ingestion.
However, ChiLCV copies significantly increased in fas2 dsRNA-fed B. tabaci.
Transmission of ChiLCV by B. tabaci was completely inhibited post-24 h feeding on hsp70 dsRNA at 3 μg/mL. Naked hsp70 dsRNA was topically sprayed on ChiLCV-infected chilli plants like an insecticide.

67.77% mortality of B. tabaci, 4.6-fold downregulation of hsp70 mRNA, and 1.34 × 1015-fold decreased ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci were recorded when adults were exposed to the dsRNA-treated plants under semi-field conditions.
Foliar application of naked dsRNA reduced the ChiLCV transmission by 75% without any visible symptoms in the inoculated plants.
A total of 2 consecutive sprays of dsRNA provided significant protection to B. tabaci for up to 20 days under semi-field conditions.

Interrupting the interrelationship between B. tabaci and begomovirus using RNAi is a promising approach.. For successful persistent-circulative transmission, the begomovirus particles need to cross the midgut barrier of B. tabaci to circulate in hemolymph and reach the primary salivary glands.

Several proteins at the midguts of B. tabaci, such as heat shock proteins (Hsp), cyclophilins, peptidoglycan recognition protein, and a midgut protein, are known to interact with begomovirus coat protein (CP) for successful internalization.
RNA-Seq of B. tabaci in response to begomoviruses revealed significant upregulations of hsp70, fasciclin 2 (fas2), and several other transcripts.
In gene regulatory network analyses, these genes were enriched with higher degrees of interactions.
The same trend was recorded in the mRNA expression in reverse transcriptase quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) post-exposure to ChiLCV.

A homogeneous population of B. tabaci developed from a single adult female was characterized by sequencing the mtCOI gene.
PCR amplification of B. tabaci mtCOI with C1-J-2195 and L2-N-3014 primers (Table 1) showed an expected amplicon of ~860 bp on an agarose gel.
The nucleotide (nt) sequence showed 99.99% homology in BLASTn analysis with other B. tabaci Asia II 1 sequences in NCBI.
The sequence can be retrieved using the GenBank Accession No. MT920041.
The identity of the virus was confirmed by sequencing the DNA-A component from infected chilli plants.
PCR amplification of the DNA-A using Begomo F and Begomo R primer produced a 2.7 kb product visualized on 1% agarose gel.
Bidirectional sequencing of the cloned products produced a 2763 nt sequence comprising complete DNA-A that showed 100% nucleotide identity to ChiLCV isolates upon BLASTn analysis.
The sequence can be retrieved by GenBank Accession No. OM513903.
Synthesis of dsRNA Targeting B. tabaci hsp70 and fas2

A conserved 128 nt-long (2416 to 2543 nt) fragment of the hsp70 gene (~2.5 kb) and a 150 nt-long (1085 to 1234 nt) fragment of the fas2 gene (~1.4 kb) of B. tabaci were selected for dsRNA designing (Figure 1a,b).
In siRNA Wizard 3.1, the 128 nt-long B. tabaci hsp70 fragment produced a putative siRNA of 21 nt (5’-GAUCCAUCCAUGCCGUUAAUC-3’).
The 150 nt-long fas2 fragment also yielded one putative siRNA of 21 nt (5’-GGACGGAAGAAGGCAUAAUCA-3’).

The dsRNA sequence was specific to B. tabaci, and no cross-reactivity was recorded with other organisms such as Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, Aves (taxid:8782), Lepidoptera (taxid:7088), Hymenoptera (taxid:7399), Formicidae (taxid:36668), and plants (taxid:3193) in BLAST analysis.
3.3. Effect of dsRNA on Mortality and mRNA Expression of B. tabaci under Controlled Conditions
Oral delivery of fas2 dsRNA at 1.0 μg/mL exhibited 39.33% mean mortality after 24 h (Figure 2b).
Significantly higher mortality (62 and 72%) of B. tabaci adults was recorded when 2.0 and 3.0 μg/mL fas2 dsRNA was orally delivered to B. tabaci under controlled laboratory conditions.
At all doses, the mortality of B. tabaci post-fas2 dsRNA exposure was significantly lower than the hsp70 dsRNA at p  <  0.05.
However, no morpho-deformities were observed in killed B. tabaci adults either with hsp70 or fas2 dsRNA.
The mRNA expression levels were significantly reduced with an increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration.
An exposure to hsp70 dsRNA at 2.0 μg/mL for 24 h significantly reduced the hsp70 mRNA expression by 11.32-fold and up to 12.85-fold when fed with 3.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA.

The fas2 mRNA expression levels were declined by 5.48-fold post-24 h feeding on fas2 dsRNA at 1.0 μg/mL. The mRNA expression levels post-hsp70 and -fas2 dsRNA feeding were almost similar at 1.0 μg/mL. The mRNA expression levels were significantly reduced up to 8.53-fold with an increase in fas2 dsRNA concentration.

The reduction in mRNA expression level was significantly higher post-hsp70 dsRNA feeding compared to fas2 dsRNA at 2.0 and 3.0 μg/mL. The primer pairs for hsp70, fas2, and β-actin did not produce any secondary peaks in the RT-qPCR melting curve analysis that indicated the specificity of the reactions (Figure 2d,e).

When B. tabaci was fed with sterile distilled water instead of hsp70 dsRNA, the mean ChiLCV copy number was 2.22 × 1015, whereas it decreased by 35.18-fold (6.31 × 1013 copies) post-exposure to hsp70 dsRNA at 1.0 μg/mL (Figure 3c).
The virus copy number in treated B. tabaci further decreased with a gradual increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration.
At 2.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA, ChiLCV copy numbers were 6.14 × 1010 in B. tabaci i.e., 3.62 × 104-fold lower than the untreated control.

The virus copies were undetectable in B. tabaci with a further increase in hsp70 dsRNA concentration to 3.0 μg/mL. The retention of ChiLCV might be completely ceased at a higher concentration of hsp70 dsRNA or beyond the detection limit using qPCR.
In contrast, the ChiLCV copy number acquired by fas2 dsRNA-treated B. tabaci was significantly higher than the untreated control (Figure 3d).

When B. tabaci was fed with sterile distilled water instead of fas2 dsRNA, the mean ChiLCV copy number was 3.19 × 1011, whereas the virus copies increased significantly by 139.18-fold (4.44 × 1013 copies) at 1.0 μg/mL of fas2 dsRNA feeding.
However, the mean virus copies were estimated to be 3.02 × 1013 and 2.14 × 1013 after exposure to 2.0 and 3.0 μg/mL fas2 dsRNA, respectively.

Although significantly higher numbers of virus copies were recorded in all fas2 dsRNA doses compared to the control, higher doses of fas2 dsRNA recorded a decline in virus copies compared to the lower doses.
All the inoculated plants produced strong leaf curl and vein-clearing symptoms and tested ChiLCV positive in PCR.

Although there was a significant decrease in ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci exposed to 1.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA, all the test plants were found to be infected with ChiLCV in PCR testing at 35 days post-inoculation.
Probably even a lower concentration of ChiLCV in B. tabaci was sufficient to make 100% transmission.
However, the severity of the leaf curl symptoms in inoculated plants was less than the untreated control.
The transmission of ChiLCV was decreased to 40% when B. tabaci were fed with 2.0 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA for 24 h (Figure 3e).
3.5. Effect of Topical Spray of hsp70 dsRNA on Mortality and Virus Transmission by B. tabaci under Semi-Field Conditions
dsRNA was not directly delivered to B. tabaci.
Instead, it was sprayed on ChiLCV-infected chilli plants, and B. tabaci adults were released on the sprayed plants.
Considering the exogenous degradation of dsRNA under natural atmospheric conditions, a ten-fold higher dose of dsRNA (30 μg/mL) than the controlled condition assay was used.
A 67.77% mortality of adult B. tabaci was recorded post-24 h exposure to dsRNA-treated plants (Figure 4a).
A 4.6-fold decrease in hsp70 mRNA expression levels of B. tabaci exposed to dsRNA-treated plants was also noted in RT-qPCR with respect to the endogenous control gene, β-actin (Figure 4b).
Specific peaks of hsp70 and β-actin in the melting curve analysis without any secondary peaks confirmed the specificity of the reactions (Figure 4c).
The surviving B. tabaci adults post-exposure to dsRNA-treated plants were further assessed for ChiLCV acquisition and transmission efficiency.
A 1.84 × 108-fold decrease in ChiLCV copies was observed in B. tabaci post-24 h exposure to ChiLCV-infected plants that were sprayed with hsp70 dsRNA at 30 μg/mL (Figure 4d).
The melt curve of ChiLCV amplicon in qPCR produced specific peaks without any secondary peaks that confirmed the specificity of the reactions (Figure 4e).

When a portion of the same B. tabaci population was used for inoculation of ChiLCV in healthy chilli plants, a 75% decrease in transmission efficiency was confirmed in PCR test (Figure 4f) with no visible symptoms in the inoculated plants up to 50 days post-inoculation (Figure 4g).

Probably, the virus titer was too low in inoculated plants to produce strong visible symptoms, whereas 100% transmission and severe leaf curl symptoms were noted in plants inoculated by unexposed B. tabaci.
No transmission of ChiLCV was recorded in the plants mock-inoculated with untreated virus-free B. tabaci.

To check the persistency in eradicating B. tabaci population by the topical spray of hsp70 dsRNA under contained semi-field conditions, fresh B. tabaci adults were released on the dsRNA-treated chilli plants at 24 h intervals.
After the first topical spray, mortality of 58.89% was recorded at 2 days.
Significant mortality (56.67%) persisted up to 8 days after the first spray (Figure 5b).
The mortality decreased to 13.33% at 10 days after the first spray.
After the second topical spray of dsRNA, the mortality percentage again rose to 75% at two days.
The highest mortality (86.67%) of B. tabaci was recorded 4 days after the second spray.
Significantly higher mortality was sustained up to 8 days after the second application and thereafter started decreasing.
Overall, 2 consecutive sprays provided substantial protection against fresh releases of B. tabaci for up to 20 days.
RNAi using dsRNA constructs is not suitable for field conditions due to rapid degradation and a lack of reliable delivery agents.
In the present study, for the first time, we demonstrated the efficacy of a naked dsRNA against an insect pest by spray-on application under semi-field conditions.
The dsRNA construct targeting the hsp70 gene of B. tabaci not only induced mortality in B. tabaci but also inhibited the transmission of ChiLCV from infected to healthy chilli plants by B. tabaci.
The fas2 mRNA expression level was upregulated in viruliferous B. tabaci by 2.6 and 4.518-fold in the RNA-Seq and RT-qPCR assay, respectively.
The Fas2 orthologue in mammals (NCAM) is known to serve as a receptor for the rabies virus.
Hence, we targeted to knock down these two genes, hsp70 and fas2, to induce immunity to ChiLCV infection in B. tabaci.

Conserved 128 and 150 nt stretches in the hsp70 and fas2 genes, respectively, were found to be specific to B. tabaci without any cross-reactivity to humans, mice, birds, butterflies, bees, ants, and plants.
Each produced a putative siRNA of 21 nt.
dsRNA was synthesized by in vivo transcription to harvest large quantities of dsRNA at a low cost.
Bacterially expressed dsRNA is economical and convenient, as reported in several studies.
Before evaluating the efficacy of topically sprayed dsRNA, we tested it under controlled laboratory conditions.
Both hsp70 and fas2 dsRNA were orally delivered to B. tabaci adults by mixing with an artificial diet in a feeding setup.
Similar types of artificial feeding setup were reported to be efficient in the oral delivery of dsRNA.
A significant knockdown of the B. tabaci population was recorded at 24 h, which gradually increased with an increase in dsRNA concentration.
Similarly, fas2 dsRNA at 3.0 μg/mL caused 72% mortality of B. tabaci 24 h post-feeding.
The dsRNA exposure downregulated the hsp70 and fas2 mRNA expressions by 12.85- and 8.53-fold, respectively.
The expression of an endogenous control gene was unregulated post-dsRNA exposure.
This indicated the specificity of the dsRNA constructs to target genes.

Hsp belongs to the multifunctional molecular chaperone family involved in the aggregation of damaged proteins, transportation, assembly, and disassembly of multi-structured units under stressed conditions.
The mortality of B. tabaci post-dsRNA feeding may be due to the loss of function via depletion of hsp70 mRNA, which might interrupt the normal biological processes in B. tabaci.
In Drosophila melanogaster, Fas2 is involved in synaptic development and growth.
It is also known to function in intracellular signaling pathways that involve mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and regulate intracellular calcium levels.
However, the function of fas2 in B. tabaci is uncharacterized.
Kanakala et al. reported twisting of wings in B. tabaci upon silencing hsp70.
However, we did not record any morphological deformities in treated B. tabaci.

Hsp70, along with other molecular chaperones, plays an important role in the translocation of viral proteins besides its function in viral replication, assembly, and disassembly of the viral proteins inside the hosts.
Hsp70 has been found to interact with TYLCV CP in vitro and co-localize within midgut epithelial cells.
In the present study, oral delivery of hsp70 dsRNA significantly reduced ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci Asia II 1 and its transmission to healthy chilli plants as well.
The resistance to ChiLCV in B. tabaci was enhanced at higher concentrations of hsp70 dsRNA.

ChiLCV copies in B. tabaci were imperceptible when B. tabaci fed on 3 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA for 24 h. The transmission of ChiLCV from infected to healthy plants by B. tabaci Asia II 1 was completely inhibited at 3 μg/mL hsp70 dsRNA treatment under controlled conditions.
Our findings are consistent with Kanakala et al., who reported the deleterious effect of B. tabaci hsp70 dsRNA on TYLCV transmission.
The TYLCV titer decreased in B. tabaci Middle East Asia Minor 1 (MEAM 1) after feeding on hsp70 dsRNA-expressing tomato plants.
Transmission of TYLCV also dropped by 12% post-silencing of hsp70.
In the present study, the inability of B. tabaci Asia II 1 to retain and transmit ChiLCV post-silencing of hsp70 indicates that it might also play an important function in ChiLCV infection.
However, Gotz et al. reported an increase in TYLCV transmission upon blocking Hsp70 by anti-Hsp70 antibody in B. tabaci MEAM1.
It was hypothesized that the Hsp70-TYLCV interaction mediates the degradation of virions.
Significantly increased transmission efficiency of CLCuV was noted in B. tabaci Asia II 1 when hsp70 was silenced.
The difference may be due to the variation in virus species and B. tabaci cryptic species.
The interactions of B. tabaci with begomoviruses are not conserved and alter with cryptic species of B. tabaci and begomovirus species.
B. tabaci MEAM1 has two genes (Bta03000 and Bta02903) annotated as hsp70, and their amino acid sequences differ by 97.55%.
They might also exhibit differential responses to begomovirus infection.
The Fas2 orthologue in mammals (NCAM) is known to serve as a receptor for the rabies virus.
Although NCAM promotes the penetration of the virus in cells, it suppresses virus replication via induction of Interferon-ß, which is mainly involved in innate immunity against viral infection.
Upregulation of fas2 transcripts in B. tabaci post-ChiLCV infection might be due to the innate immune response against the virus infection.
We hypothesized that fas2 has a negative regulatory role in ChiLCV infection, and thus, knocking down fas2 increased the virus titer in B. tabaci.
Hence, silencing fas2 was not considered to induce resistance to ChiLCV despite its efficacy in eradicating B. tabaci.
Although RNAi has emerged as a promising alternative to suppress crop pests, there are limitations in the application of dsRNA as a ‘spray-on’ technology for field use.
Reduced stability in the extracellular environments of dsRNA contributes to poor RNAi response.
The naked dsRNA quickly degrades in higher temperatures and UV radiation under natural environmental conditions.
Besides, several insect species, mainly lepidopteran insects, have been observed to be refractory to RNAi due to degradation and poor intracellular transport of exogenous dsRNA.
In the first phase of the study, hsp70 dsRNA showed high potential in eradicating B. tabaci and inhibiting ChiLCV transmission.
In the next phase, the dsRNA construct was assessed under natural environmental conditions by spraying like an insecticide.
Adult B. tabaci are highly mobile, so spraying on adult flies was not preferred.
Hence, naked hsp70 dsRNA without any delivery agent was topically sprayed onto the foliage of the ChiLCV-infected chilli plant under contained semi-field conditions.
B. tabaci adults were released on the dsRNA-sprayed plants to evaluate the dsRNA’s efficacy in eradicating B. tabaci and inhibiting the transmission of ChiLCV.
Considering the extracellular degradation of dsRNA and delivery through the host plant, a 10-fold higher dose than the controlled assay was used for topical application.
A 67.77% mortality with a 4.6-fold decrease in hsp70 mRNA levels in B. tabaci exposed to the dsRNA-sprayed plants was noted after 24 h of release.
Further, 1.84 × 108-fold decreased ChiLCV copies and 75% reduced transmission of ChiLCV indicated the efficiency of topically sprayed hsp70 dsRNA in managing both the virus and its vector.
Although the efficacy of topically applied naked dsRNA against plant viruses is known, this is the first evidence of its efficacy against a hemipteran insect like B. tabaci.
Topical application of dsRNA could provide resistance for 12 to 21 days against plant viruses.
In the present study, dsRNA was detected in the leaf tissues up to 6 h post-application.
Significant mortality of B. tabaci on the treated plants persisted up to 8 days and was further sustained up to 20 days with a second spray on the 10th day.
Protection of the plants during the early growth stage is crucial in the management of begomoviruses.
In conclusion, the spray-on application of naked dsRNA targeting hsp70 of B. tabaci provides resistance to both ChiLCV and its vector, B. tabaci.
This is a novel alternative to hazardous insecticides and may be further assessed on a large scale for its efficacy under real-field conditions.
